title: The 2026 Midterms, in context
text: Midterms are a national referendum with 435 local House contests, a smaller but consequential Senate map, and turnout that tends to lag presidential years. This edition pairs historical House results with an illustrative 2026 scenario: modeled figures are not reported polls, fundraising disclosures, or election returns.

title: The 2026 Midterms, in context
text:
The midterm pattern
The president’s party has usually lost House seats at the first election between presidential contests. The exceptions matter: national conditions, candidate quality, district boundaries, and the particular seats at stake can all overwhelm the average. The bars below show the House seat change for the president’s party; the line smooths the record with a five-election rolling average.







Historical series: net change in House seats for the president’s party at each midterm, compiled from official election results. A negative value is a loss. The rolling line begins after five observations.

Races to watch

title: The 2026 Midterms, in context
text:
How to read this edition
The historical chart is retrospective; the battleground comparisons and turnout page are planning scenarios, not a forecast or a statement of certified 2026 outcomes. A projected margin is measured in percentage points, with positive values favoring the Democratic candidate in the scenario. Replace the scenario inputs with linked, dated sources before using them as current reporting.






Note



A note on uncertainty. A generic margin-of-error band is not a substitute for a poll’s sample design, field dates, likely-voter model, or aggregation method. Scenario inputs on this site are labeled as such and should not be read as polling.

title: Who votes—and who might turn out?
text: Midterm participation is uneven. Age, education, and where a person lives are associated with different turnout rates, but the differences are not fixed from one election to the next. The chart combines rounded, illustrative benchmark estimates for 2018 and 2022 with a modeled 2026 scenario. None should be read as certified official demographic counts.

title: Who votes—and who might turn out?
text:
Participation by group
The bars compare each group’s estimated turnout in the three midterm cycles. The 2026 values are scenario projections, not exit polls or post-election estimates. Group categories are broad and can conceal large differences within each group.












Important



Projection ≠ result. The 2026 bars show a scenario assumption only. Turnout estimates depend on the population denominator, eligibility rules, survey design, and whether rates are measured among citizens, voting-age residents, or eligible voters.

title: Who votes—and who might turn out?
text:
What the comparison can—and cannot—show

Age: Older voters tend to participate at higher rates in midterms, so shifts in the age mix of the electorate can change the overall result even when group-level preferences stay constant.
Education: Educational attainment is associated with participation, but it is also correlated with age, income, geography, and other factors. These bars do not isolate a causal effect.
Community type: Urban, suburban, and rural categories vary by definition and state. A national-style comparison can hide important local patterns.
2026: Treat the final column as a transparent placeholder for a forecast. Replace it with a named, dated, documented source before drawing conclusions about the actual electorate.


The demographic values are deliberately rounded, synthetic examples. They are not sourced estimates, survey results, Census counts, or certified 2026 turnout. The chart demonstrates a comparison workflow and should be updated with documented data before publication as factual analysis.

title: Battlegrounds: the close contests
text: The map is a mix of statewide Senate contests and competitive House districts. The figures below are synthetic scenario inputs designed to show how to compare races: they are not actual polls, campaign disclosures, or official Cook Political Report ratings. “Rating” is a Cook-style label for this demonstration only.

title: Battlegrounds: the close contests
text:
Margin and uncertainty
The dot is the scenario’s Democratic two-party margin; positive values favor the Democratic candidate. The horizontal interval shows an assumed ±4-point uncertainty band, not a poll’s published margin of error.

title: Battlegrounds: the close contests
text:
Fundraising and modeled vote share
Each point is a race. The horizontal axis combines both candidates’ scenario fundraising totals; the vertical axis translates the assumed margin into a Democratic two-party vote share. A larger combined fundraising total does not imply a closer race or a causal effect on vote share.







All margins, uncertainty bands, fundraising totals, modeled shares, and ratings in these charts are fabricated for demonstration. State/race labels identify plausible contest types; candidates are intentionally unnamed. Fundraising is in illustrative millions of dollars, with no claim about actual receipts or disbursements.
